paras: The whitecap death notice to Garfield Williams was a written threat, dated September 7, 1903, ordering Williams, a Black tenant farmer near Linwood in Pike County, Alabama, to leave within five days or be killed. No harm to Williams is reported, but the notice became government evidence in a federal whitecapping prosecution of white men from the neighborhood. In January 1904 a federal grand jury indicted five of them for attempting to oppress Williams and nine other Black people because of their race.

Williams was a tenant and farm hand of James Daniels, a white farmer in the Cross Roads and Linwood beats, about twelve miles north of Troy. According to government witnesses, Black churches in those beats had been burned, Black residents whipped and told to leave, and houses shot into, among them that of Mary Clements, who was shot with her baby in her arms as she fled. The indictment later dated this campaign from early 1902 until September 1903, when federal authorities took up the matter.

The notice to Williams was left on his doorstep. It told him to "square up your business and get out from here at once," to pay any debts, and to go twenty-five miles away within five days, "or death will be your portion." "We intend to kill you if you stay around over five days," it continued, and it was signed "The W. C. of I. and C.," with a dagger and a heart drawn beneath.

Other notices in the neighborhood were signed "Negro Skinners," "Negro Killers" or with initials, and one bore a crudely drawn heart and dagger, according to the Montgomery Advertiser. The coverage does not say whether Williams left his place.

Deputy Marshal J. F. Green arrested six white farmers, Boss Riley, Will Pitman, Tumps Chesser and Robert, John and Fletcher Windham, in late October, and they were released on $500 temporary bail. Federal officers acted because the whitecapping was thought to violate section 5508 of the Revised Statutes. At the preliminary hearing before U.S. Commissioner Tutwiler in Troy on October 30 and 31, James Daniels was among the principal government witnesses, and the notice to Williams was read into evidence. Robert Windham was discharged, Fletcher Windham was held on $750 bail and the others on $500 each for the federal grand jury.

On January 27, 1904, the grand jury returned four indictments against Riley, William Pittman and the three Windhams, Robert included, charging attempts to oppress Williams, Clements, Joe Browning and seven others "because they are of African descent." Chesser was not named among those indicted. The cases were set for the May term, and no report of a trial or its outcome was found.

The Montgomery Advertiser alone printed Williams's notice, in a Troy special headed "Held to Grand Jury" that described "rather startling conditions" in the beats. Its correspondent called Williams "a good farm hand and inoffensive" and wrote that the county's "best element" opposed such crimes because they crippled farming. Shorter versions of the bound-over news ran in the Birmingham Age-Herald and the Atlanta Constitution, without Williams's name. The indictments reached New York by telegraph, where the Tribune headed them "Blacks Caught It Hard" and listed Williams among the victims.

In the Black press, the St. Paul Appeal summarized the Troy hearing under "Afro-Americans White-capped. A Tale of Horror." in a monthly column of crimes by white people meant to show there was "no color line in crime." The Appeal stressed the shooting of Mary Clements and the flight of a sawmill's hands, and estimated that 150 people had left the county, but it did not name Garfield Williams.

reader.title: Whitecap death notice to Garfield Williams
bases: Williams was ordered by a written notice signed with the initials of an apparent band to leave within five days on pain of death, one of a series of whitecap notices, burnings and shootings in the Linwood and Cross Roads beats that were prosecuted federally as whitecapping (A4, A9, A10).
The notice threatened Williams with death but no report says he was attacked, injured or killed (A4, A9, A10); the episode is a threat by an apparent band, not a killing.

The text of the notice appears only in the Troy hearing report (A4), but the January 1904 indictments, reported separately in Montgomery and by telegraph to New York, independently name Garfield Williams, farm hand of James Daniels, among those the accused threatened (A9, A10).

accounts.gist: The notice to Williams was read into evidence among several threatening notes; it ordered him to leave within five days or be killed and was signed 'The W. C. of I. and C.'

accounts.label: Federal indictment
accounts.gist: The grand jury charged five white men with threatening Williams and nine other Black people, their property and lives, unless they left the Linwood community, because they were Black.

accounts.gist: A Birmingham item summarized the hearing's evidence of church burnings, shootings and the flight of the sawmill hands, without naming Williams.

framing.detail: The Montgomery Advertiser headed its report 'Held to Grand Jury' and described 'rather startling conditions' and the notice's target as 'inoffensive', while stressing harm to farming interests.
The New-York Tribune ran the indictment under 'Blacks Caught It Hard. Alabama White Men Now Indicted for Whitecapping.'
The St. Paul Appeal placed the hearing under 'Afro-Americans White-capped. A Tale of Horror.' in a column meant to show there was 'no color line in crime'.
